method: Each lens is a weighted mean of 0–100 criteria; “lower adds” criteria use 100 minus the value. Leaders are scored on twelve-axis criteria only; scores need at least two criteria with data. Placements and lenses are editorial interpretations.

authors.name: George Orwell
authors.works: Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), Animal Farm (1945), Homage to Catalonia (1938)
authors.idea: A democratic socialist who spent his life warning that any ideology, left or right, can end in a state that controls truth itself.

lens.name: Big Brother Index
lens.question: How close is this place to Oceania: one Party, a rewritten record, the Thought Police and endless war?

criteria.why: One Party rules Oceania and no opposition can win.
The Ministry of Truth rewrites the record and controls what may be said.
“False information” laws let the state decide what is true.
Cutting off outside sources keeps citizens inside the Party’s version of reality.
Every channel is watched; there is no private way out.
The Thought Police patrol behaviour in public.
Big Brother: the cult of one leader.
Surveillance and order over liberty.
Oceania is always at war; war keeps the population in line.
Enemies of the Party are “vaporised”.

authors.name: Aldous Huxley
authors.works: Brave New World (1932), Brave New World Revisited (1958), Island (1962)
authors.idea: Feared that people would be controlled not by pain but by pleasure, consumption and distraction.

lens.name: Brave New World Index
lens.question: How close is this place to Huxley’s World State, where people are kept content rather than free?

criteria.why: Casual sex is encouraged; pleasure replaces private attachment.
Soma: a legal drug that keeps everyone content.
Consumption is a civic duty.
Stability is the supreme value.
Ten World Controllers run everything from the centre.
No one votes; contentment makes politics unnecessary.
Religion is replaced by the worship of Ford.

authors.name: Ray Bradbury
authors.works: Fahrenheit 451 (1953), The Martian Chronicles (1950)
authors.idea: Warned of a society that burns books so that no one is ever offended or troubled by an idea.

lens.name: Fahrenheit 451 Index
lens.question: How far does this place censor ideas, books and speech?

criteria.why: Firemen burn books so no one meets a dangerous idea.
Ideas are banned to protect feelings, as blasphemy laws protect faith.
The state decides what information may circulate.
Criticising rulers is a crime.
Order over intellectual freedom.

authors.name: Margaret Atwood
authors.works: The Handmaid’s Tale (1985), The Testaments (2019), Oryx and Crake (2003)
authors.idea: Imagined Gilead, a theocracy that strips women of property, reading and control of their own bodies — built only from things that had happened somewhere.

lens.name: Gilead Index
lens.question: How close is this place to Gilead, where religion rules and women’s bodies belong to the state?

criteria.why: Reproduction is controlled by the state.
Women may not read, own property or work.
Women wear assigned religious dress.
Adultery is punished by the state.
Gay people are executed as “gender traitors”.
A theocracy governs in the name of scripture.
Women are given in marriage by men.
criteria.data: Law: Male guardian for a bride

criteria.why: Death for private conduct.

authors.name: Yevgeny Zamyatin
authors.idea: His One State, where people live in glass houses and every hour is scheduled, inspired both Huxley and Orwell.

lens.name: One State Index
lens.question: How close is this place to the One State of We, where life is planned and the Benefactor is elected unanimously?

criteria.why: The One State schedules every hour of every citizen’s day.
Freedom is called the root of crime; the Guardians watch.
Production and life follow the Table of Hours.
The Benefactor is re-elected unanimously every year.
Even sex is scheduled, with pink tickets.
Dissenters are liquidated by the Benefactor’s Machine.

authors.name: Franz Kafka
authors.works: The Trial (1925), The Castle (1926), In the Penal Colony (1919)
authors.idea: Described people crushed by an opaque, unaccountable authority that never explains itself.

lens.name: Kafka Index
lens.question: How unaccountable and opaque is authority here?

criteria.why: No one may learn or say what the charge is.
Offending authority is itself an offence.
Punishment arrives without visible justice.
Power answers to no one.
No higher court, no appeal, no exit.
A vast, distant bureaucracy decides.

authors.name: Kurt Vonnegut
authors.works: Harrison Bergeron (1961), Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), Player Piano (1952)
authors.idea: A humanist who satirised a future where equality is enforced by handicapping anyone above average.

lens.name: Handicapper General Index
lens.question: How far does this place enforce sameness from the centre?

criteria.why: Everyone is made equal by law.
Agents enforce the handicaps.
The United States Handicapper General.
Talent is levelled down by the state.

authors.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
authors.works: The Brothers Karamazov (1880), Demons (1872), Crime and Punishment (1866)
authors.idea: An Orthodox believer who feared that people would trade freedom for bread, and that revolutionaries without God would justify anything.

lens.name: Grand Inquisitor Index
lens.question: How far does the state give bread, faith and authority in exchange for freedom, as the Grand Inquisitor did?

criteria.why: “Bread”: the Inquisitor feeds the people.
“Mystery”: faith administered by an institution.
“Authority”: a few decide so the many need not choose.
Freedom is taken away as a burden.
Doubting the official faith is punished.
The people surrender choice.

authors.name: Leo Tolstoy
authors.works: War and Peace (1869), The Kingdom of God Is Within You (1894), Resurrection (1899)
authors.idea: A Christian anarchist who rejected all violence, including the state’s armies, prisons and executions.

lens.name: Tolstoyan Non-violence
lens.question: How far does this place renounce force, executions and conscription?

criteria.why: Do not resist evil by force.
He condemned executions and prisons.
He urged refusal of military service.
Government is organised violence.
Peasant communities, not the state.
Simple living on the land.

authors.name: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
authors.works: The Gulag Archipelago (1973), One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (1962)
authors.idea: Survivor of the Soviet camps who documented them, and a Russian Orthodox traditionalist.

lens.name: Gulag Test
lens.question: How close is this place to a one-party state that imprisons dissent and persecutes belief?

criteria.why: One party ruled and imprisoned millions.
Believers were persecuted.
Article 58 punished “anti-Soviet agitation”.
Executions and deaths in the camps.
Writers were silenced.
Order through fear.

authors.name: Václav Havel
authors.works: The Power of the Powerless (1978), Letters to Olga (1988)
authors.idea: Dissident playwright, later president, who said a regime of lies falls when ordinary people refuse to live within them.

lens.name: Living in Truth
lens.question: Can ordinary people say what is true and remove those in power?

criteria.why: The greengrocer can take the slogan out of his window.
Power must answer to citizens.
Mocking power is not a crime.
The power of the powerless, not of one leader.
Civil society and local initiative.

authors.name: Hannah Arendt
authors.works: The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951), Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963), The Human Condition (1958)
authors.idea: Explained how totalitarianism uses ideology, terror and isolation, and how ordinary officials carry out great evil.

lens.name: Totalitarian Elements
lens.question: How many of the elements of totalitarian rule does this place show?

criteria.why: One movement absorbs the state.
A designated enemy group is persecuted.
Terror is the essence of the regime.
Ideology replaces reality.
The leader principle.
Tribal nationalism.
The masses are isolated from the world.

authors.name: Karl Popper
authors.works: The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), The Poverty of Historicism (1957)
authors.idea: Defended the open society, where rulers can be removed without bloodshed and every idea can be criticised.

lens.name: Open Society
lens.question: Can people criticise power and remove rulers without bloodshed?

criteria.why: Democracy is the power to remove rulers peacefully.
Criticism is how societies correct mistakes.
No one holds the final truth.
Institutions, not great leaders.
Freedom of thought.

authors.name: Isaiah Berlin
authors.works: Two Concepts of Liberty (1958), The Hedgehog and the Fox (1953)
authors.idea: Distinguished freedom from interference from the dangerous promise of a “true” self imposed by the state.

lens.name: Negative Liberty
lens.question: How large is the area in which people are left alone?

criteria.why: An area where a person is left alone.
Freedom to choose one’s own ends.
Freedom of expression.
Absence of coercion.
Pluralism of values and faiths.

authors.name: John Stuart Mill
authors.works: On Liberty (1859), The Subjection of Women (1869), Utilitarianism (1863)
authors.idea: Argued that the state may restrict a person only to prevent harm to others.

lens.name: Harm Principle
lens.question: Does the law leave people sovereign over their own lives, bodies and opinions?

criteria.why: Self-regarding conduct is no business of the state.
Silencing an opinion robs the human race.
“Experiments in living.”
Private conduct between adults.
The Subjection of Women.

authors.name: John Locke
authors.works: Two Treatises of Government (1689), A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689)
authors.idea: Government exists by consent to protect life, liberty and property, and may be replaced if it does not.

lens.name: Lockean Rights
lens.question: Does government rest on consent, protect property and tolerate faiths?

criteria.why: Government by consent; the people may replace it.
Property as a natural right.
A Letter Concerning Toleration.
Limited government.
Life, liberty and estate.

authors.name: Montesquieu
authors.works: The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Persian Letters (1721)
authors.idea: Freedom survives only where legislative, executive and judicial power are separated.

lens.name: Separation of Powers
lens.question: Is power divided and checked, and are punishments moderate?

criteria.why: Power must check power.
Moderate government.
Punishments proportionate to crimes.
Intermediate powers between ruler and people.

authors.name: Voltaire
authors.works: Candide (1759), Treatise on Tolerance (1763), Philosophical Dictionary (1764)
authors.idea: Campaigned against religious persecution, censorship and judicial cruelty.

lens.name: Tolerance
lens.question: Are people free to believe, doubt and speak, without cruel punishment?

criteria.why: Treatise on Tolerance, written after the Calas affair.
He defended people prosecuted for blasphemy.
Free thought and a free press.
Against clerical power.
Against torture and judicial cruelty.

authors.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
authors.works: Democracy in America (1835–40), The Old Regime and the Revolution (1856)
authors.idea: Saw local self-government, voluntary associations and a free press as the defences against a tyranny of the majority.

lens.name: Democracy in America
lens.question: Is democracy local, associational and protected against the majority’s tyranny?

criteria.why: Township self-government and associations.
Equality of conditions with free institutions.
Religious freedom.
A free press against the tyranny of the majority.

authors.name: Adam Smith
authors.works: The Wealth of Nations (1776), The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759)
authors.idea: Showed how free exchange and the division of labour create wealth, and warned against merchants colluding with rulers.

lens.name: Wealth of Nations
lens.question: Are trade and enterprise free, and is justice secure?

criteria.why: Free trade enriches nations; mercantilism impoverishes them.
Markets coordinate millions of choices.
Justice is the main pillar of society.
Wary of collusion between merchants and rulers.

authors.name: Friedrich Hayek
authors.works: The Road to Serfdom (1944), The Constitution of Liberty (1960)
authors.idea: Argued that central economic planning leads step by step to political tyranny.

lens.name: Road to Serfdom
lens.question: How far down the road from economic planning to political control has this place gone?

criteria.why: Central planning concentrates economic power in the state.
Decisions taken centrally instead of by millions of people.
Controls on trade and prices.
Planning means “the worst get on top”.
Control of the economy becomes control of life.

authors.name: Ayn Rand
authors.works: Atlas Shrugged (1957), The Fountainhead (1943), Anthem (1938)
authors.idea: Championed rational self-interest and laissez-faire capitalism against altruism and the welfare state.

lens.name: Atlas Shrugged
lens.question: How close is this place to laissez-faire capitalism with no forced altruism?

criteria.why: Laissez-faire capitalism.
No one may be forced to serve others’ needs.
Reason, not faith.
Individual rights against force.
Free trade.

authors.name: Robert Nozick
authors.works: Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974)
authors.idea: Defended a minimal state limited to protection and contracts; anything more violates rights.

lens.name: Minimal State
lens.question: How close is this place to a state that only protects rights?

criteria.why: Taxing earnings is on a par with forced labour.
Free exchange is just.
Rights as side constraints.
A framework for voluntary utopias.
Minimal central authority.

authors.name: John Rawls
authors.works: A Theory of Justice (1971), Political Liberalism (1993)
authors.idea: Asked what society you would choose behind a “veil of ignorance”, not knowing who you would be born as.

lens.name: Veil of Ignorance
lens.question: Would you choose to be born here not knowing your sex, faith, sexuality or wealth?

criteria.why: Inequalities must benefit the worst off.
Equal basic liberties for all.
Equal basic liberties for all.
Liberty of conscience.
Fair value of political liberties.
Freedom of thought.

authors.name: John Maynard Keynes
authors.works: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936), The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919)
authors.idea: Argued that governments must manage demand to prevent mass unemployment, and helped design Bretton Woods.

lens.name: Managed Capitalism
lens.question: How close is this place to a market economy steered by the state, open to the world?

criteria.why: A market economy steered by government.
Public spending to keep employment high.
International cooperation on trade.
Multilateral institutions like the IMF and World Bank.

authors.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
authors.works: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792)
authors.idea: Argued that women are rational beings owed the same education and rights as men.

lens.name: Rights of Woman
lens.question: Do women have equal standing in law, marriage and property?

criteria.why: Equal rights for women.
Marriage as a partnership, not ownership.
Against marrying girls young.
Equal standing in law.
Women’s property.

authors.name: Simone de Beauvoir
authors.works: The Second Sex (1949), The Mandarins (1954)
authors.idea: Showed how womanhood is shaped by society, and fought for women’s economic and sexual freedom.

lens.name: The Second Sex
lens.question: Are women free in law, marriage, sexuality and reproduction?

criteria.why: Woman is made by society, not born.
She signed the 1971 Manifesto of the 343 for abortion rights.
Sexual freedom.
Against marriage as dependency.
Existentialist atheism.

authors.name: Thomas Hobbes
authors.works: Leviathan (1651)
authors.idea: Without a sovereign strong enough to keep peace, life is a war of all against all.
authors.quote: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.

lens.name: Leviathan
lens.question: How strong and undivided is the sovereign that keeps the peace?

criteria.why: An absolute sovereign to end the war of all against all.
Sovereignty must be undivided.
Security before liberty.

authors.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
authors.works: The Prince (1532), Discourses on Livy (1531)
authors.idea: Described how rulers actually win and keep power, separating politics from conventional morality.

lens.name: The Prince
lens.question: How far does this state follow the Prince’s advice: be feared, rely on your own arms, secure the state first?

criteria.why: Better to be feared than loved, if one cannot be both.
A prince must study war.
The security of the state comes first.
Unify and free the homeland.
Rely on your own arms, not allies or mercenaries.

authors.name: Edmund Burke
authors.works: Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790)
authors.idea: Defended inherited institutions and gradual reform against revolutionary schemes built on abstract reason.
authors.quote: The little platoon we belong to in society.

lens.name: Burkean Tradition
lens.question: Does this place preserve tradition and faith while keeping constitutional, limited government?

criteria.why: Society is a partnership of the dead, the living and the unborn.
Established religion as a pillar of society.
Constitutional government, not revolution.
“Little platoons”, not a centralised state.
Against arbitrary power.

authors.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
authors.works: The Social Contract (1762), Discourse on Inequality (1755), Emile (1762)
authors.idea: Legitimate power comes only from the general will of a free and equal people.
authors.quote: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.

lens.name: General Will
lens.question: Does the people rule directly, as equals, in a small and frugal republic?

criteria.why: Sovereignty cannot be represented; small republics.
No citizen rich enough to buy another, none so poor as to sell himself.
Sovereignty of the people.
Distrust of luxury and commerce.
Civic patriotism and a civil religion.

authors.name: Plato
authors.works: The Republic, The Laws
authors.idea: Imagined a city ruled by philosopher-kings, with guardians who own nothing and poets who are censored.

lens.name: Kallipolis
lens.question: How close is this place to rule by a guardian elite, with censored arts and no democracy?

criteria.why: Rule by philosopher-kings.
Guardians keep order.
Poets are censored.
Guardians own no property.
Democracy degenerates into tyranny.

authors.name: Aristotle
authors.works: Politics, Nicomachean Ethics
authors.idea: The best practical constitution is a “polity” resting on a large middle class and the rule of law, avoiding extremes.

lens.name: Polity of the Mean
lens.question: Does this place avoid extremes, with a strong middle and the rule of law?

criteria.why: Virtue lies in the mean between extremes.
criteria.data: Closeness to the middle of all twelve Compass axes

criteria.why: Rule of law and a mixed constitution.
A large middle class makes a stable state.

authors.name: Karl Marx
authors.works: The Communist Manifesto (1848, with Engels), Capital (1867)
authors.idea: History is a story of class struggle; workers would abolish private ownership of the means of production.

lens.name: Communist Manifesto
lens.question: How close is this economy and society to the Manifesto’s aims?

criteria.why: Abolition of private ownership of the means of production.
From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.
Religion as “the opium of the people”.
The working men have no country.

authors.name: Peter Kropotkin
authors.works: Mutual Aid (1902), The Conquest of Bread (1892)
authors.idea: Anarchist geographer who argued that cooperation, not competition, drives survival, and that free communes could replace the state.

lens.name: Mutual Aid
lens.question: How far is power local, cooperative and free of coercion?

criteria.why: Free federations of communes.
No rulers.
Bread for all.
No coercive state.
He wanted prisons abolished.

authors.name: John Steinbeck
authors.works: The Grapes of Wrath (1939), Of Mice and Men (1937)
authors.idea: Told the story of migrant farm workers driven off their land and exploited.

lens.name: Grapes of Wrath
lens.question: Would the Joads find dignity here?

criteria.why: Dignity and support for migrant workers.
“Okies” were treated as foreigners in their own land.
The Dust Bowl came from over-farming.
Against banks and landowners squeezing tenants.

authors.name: Charles Dickens
authors.works: Oliver Twist (1838), Hard Times (1854), Bleak House (1853)
authors.idea: Exposed workhouses, child labour, debtors’ prisons and the cruelty of a system that forgot the poor.

lens.name: Hard Times Test
lens.question: Does this place protect the poor and children?
lens.top: A society that cares for Oliver

criteria.why: Against workhouses and child labour.
Against cruel schoolmasters like Squeers in Nicholas Nickleby.
Children and families protected.
Against debtors’ prisons and harsh courts.

authors.name: Victor Hugo
authors.works: Les Misérables (1862), The Last Day of a Condemned Man (1829)
authors.idea: Campaigned against the death penalty and showed how poverty and harsh law crush people like Jean Valjean.

lens.name: Les Misérables Test
lens.question: Does justice here show mercy, and does society relieve poverty?

criteria.why: Against harsh punishment.
He campaigned to abolish the death penalty.
Poverty breeds crime.

authors.name: Frantz Fanon
authors.works: The Wretched of the Earth (1961), Black Skin, White Masks (1952)
authors.idea: Psychiatrist of colonialism who argued for full decolonisation, and warned against a new national elite replacing the old one.

lens.name: Decolonisation
lens.question: Is this nation economically and politically free of outside domination?

criteria.why: Freedom from foreign domination.
Against a national bourgeoisie that serves outside capital.
Land and resources for the peasants.
Economic self-reliance.

authors.name: Henry David Thoreau
authors.works: Walden (1854), Civil Disobedience (1849)
authors.idea: Went to jail rather than pay taxes for slavery and war, and lived simply in the woods.
authors.quote: In wildness is the preservation of the world.

lens.name: Walden
lens.question: Does government govern little, avoid war and leave nature wild?

criteria.why: In wildness is the preservation of the world.
That government is best which governs least.
He refused taxes for the Mexican War.
Conscience above the law.

authors.name: Rachel Carson
authors.works: Silent Spring (1962), The Sea Around Us (1951)
authors.idea: Showed how pesticides poison birds, water and people, and started the modern environmental movement.

lens.name: Silent Spring
lens.question: Does this place put ecology before industrial growth?

criteria.why: Protect nature from industrial poisons.
Pollution crosses every border.

authors.name: Rabindranath Tagore
authors.works: Gitanjali (1910), Nationalism (1917), The Home and the World (1916)
authors.idea: Nobel laureate who warned that the nation-state organises selfishness, and dreamed of a mind without fear.

lens.name: Where the Mind Is Without Fear
lens.question: Is this place free of fear, aggressive nationalism and militarism?

criteria.why: Nationalism (1917): the nation as organised selfishness.
Universal humanism; Visva-Bharati, a university for the world.
Against militarism.
Where the mind is without fear.
Education in nature at Santiniketan.

authors.name: Mahatma Gandhi
authors.works: Hind Swaraj (1909), The Story of My Experiments with Truth (1927)
authors.idea: Non-violence, village self-rule, swadeshi and equal respect for all religions.

lens.name: Hind Swaraj
lens.question: Is this place non-violent, self-reliant, local and tolerant of all faiths?

criteria.why: Ahimsa: non-violence.
Village self-rule.
Swadeshi.
Simple living and local production.
Equal respect for all religions.
Against the death penalty.

authors.name: B. R. Ambedkar
authors.works: Annihilation of Caste (1936), The Problem of the Rupee (1923), Who Were the Shudras? (1946)
authors.idea: Argued that political democracy must rest on social democracy — liberty, equality and fraternity — and that caste must be destroyed.

lens.name: Annihilation of Caste
lens.question: Does this place guarantee equal rights, freedom of conscience and the freedom to marry across lines?

criteria.why: The Hindu Code Bill for women’s rights.
Freedom of conscience; he left Hinduism for Buddhism.
State socialism for economic democracy.
Constitutional democracy.
Inter-marriage as the real remedy for caste.
Against hierarchy sanctioned by tradition.

authors.name: Chanakya (Kautilya)
authors.works: Arthashastra
authors.idea: Minister to Chandragupta Maurya whose Arthashastra sets out statecraft: a rich treasury, spies, realist diplomacy and the welfare of subjects.

lens.name: Arthashastra Statecraft
lens.question: How closely does this state follow Kautilya: a strong centre, watchful spies, realist force abroad and care for subjects?

criteria.why: A strong central treasury and administration.
Spies watch officials and subjects.
The mandala: a neighbour is a natural enemy; diplomacy is backed by force.
The state’s own interest decides foreign policy.
In the happiness of his subjects lies the king’s happiness.

authors.name: Thiruvalluvar
authors.works: Thirukkural
authors.idea: The Kural’s book on wealth describes the just king: protective, generous, open to criticism and never cruel.

lens.name: The Just Sceptre
lens.question: Is rule here protective, merciful and open to criticism?

criteria.why: The king protects and provides for his people.
The cruel sceptre ruins the kingdom.
A ruler should heed counsel.
The world shelters under the king who can bear bitter words.

authors.name: Confucius
authors.works: The Analects
authors.idea: Order rests on virtue, ritual and family duty; rulers should lead by example rather than punishment.

lens.name: Confucian Order
lens.question: Does order here rest on family, ritual and moral example rather than punishment?

criteria.why: Ritual, filial piety and family hierarchy.
Harmony and social order.
Lead by virtue, not by punishments.
Rule by moral example.
The ruler cares for the people.

authors.name: Laozi
authors.works: Tao Te Ching
authors.idea: The best government acts little and lets people be; weapons and laws multiply troubles.

lens.name: Wu Wei
lens.question: Does government here act little and let people and nature be?

criteria.why: Do not stir the small fish.
The best ruler is barely known.
Weapons are instruments of ill omen.
The more laws, the more thieves.
Harmony with nature.
Let people be.

authors.name: Mencius
authors.works: Mencius
authors.idea: Benevolent government feeds the people; a tyrant who does not has lost the mandate of Heaven and may be removed.

lens.name: Benevolent Government
lens.question: Does the ruler feed the people, tax lightly and accept that a tyrant may be removed?

criteria.why: Rulers must ensure the people have land and food.
Heaven sees as the people see; a tyrant may be removed.
Light punishments.
Against wars of conquest.

authors.name: Han Feizi
authors.works: Han Feizi
authors.idea: The Legalist: people are governed by clear laws, heavy punishments and a ruler who trusts no one.

lens.name: Legalist State
lens.question: How far does this state govern by strict law, heavy punishment and central control?

criteria.why: Strict laws and heavy punishments.
All power to the ruler.
Techniques of control over ministers.
Law and order over individual will.

authors.name: Mozi
authors.works: Mozi
authors.idea: Taught impartial care for all and condemned wars of aggression and wasteful luxury.

lens.name: Universal Care
lens.question: Does this state avoid aggression and spend on people rather than display?

criteria.why: Condemn offensive war.
Benefit all people.
Frugality, against waste.

authors.name: Ibn Khaldun
authors.works: Muqaddimah (1377)
authors.idea: States rise on group solidarity (asabiyyah) and decline in luxury, heavy taxes and arbitrary rule.

lens.name: Asabiyyah
lens.question: Does this state show the solidarity and light taxation of a rising power?

criteria.why: Group feeling binds a people.
Religion strengthens group feeling.
Low taxes bring high revenue; heavy taxes kill enterprise.
Absolute, luxurious rule brings decline.
